claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles depends on synchronized reduction and nucleation of all metal precursors.
Synchronizing precursor reduction minimizes differences in reduction kinetics and enables simultaneous atomic mixing.
Simultaneous atomic mixing favors homogeneous alloy formation over phase separation or elemental segregation.
A moderate thermal ramp rate can synchronize reduction of the metal precursors.
Transient metastable surface atomic clusters form during reduction.
Transient metastable surface atomic clusters facilitate rapid interdiffusion.
Simultaneously reduced nascent metal atoms mix rapidly enough to overcome thermodynamic driving forces toward phase separation.
An uncontrolled or excessively fast thermal ramp causes staggered precursor reduction and nucleation at different times.
Staggered reduction and nucleation promote phase separation or elemental segregation.
An optimized moderate ramp will produce nanoparticles with a homogeneously mixed high-entropy alloy structure.
Nanoparticles produced under the optimized moderate ramp will retain high surface-atom exposure.
Relative to the moderate ramp, a rapid heating baseline will exhibit more phase separation, elemental clustering, and non-uniform morphology.
A rapid heating protocol produces unsynchronized reduction, undesirable segregation, and higher apparent decomposition temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies mainly to noble metal multicomponent systems whose precursor reduction potentials are relatively comparable.
The mechanism may fail when precursor reduction kinetics differ so greatly that moderated heating cannot induce simultaneous nucleation.
